newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House set to vote on tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House set to vote on tax cut bill.

text.p: The U.S. Congress debated legislation Thursday aimed at giving Americans the biggest tax cut in 16 years, with arguments among the two parties centred on who would benefit the most.

The House of Representatives was expected to vote on its bill in the afternoon, while the Senate debate was likely to continue well into the evening. Differences in the two bills must ultimately be ironed out before final legislation can be sent to President Clinton.

The legislation would implement the tax portion of the balanced budget agreement reached by congressional leaders and the White House last month which called for $85 billion in net tax cuts over five years.
The White House has problems with provisions in both bills, but found the Senate plan less objectionable than the one before the House.

Democrats criticised the Republican bill as giving too big a share of the tax relief to the wealthy. "Democrats always want to reduce taxes, but they want to do it fairly," Representative Jim McDermott, a Washington Democrat, said.

Republicans stressed the bulk of the tax relief would go to the middle class. "It's unfortunate we have to deal with this economic class warfare rhetoric over and over again," House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer said. "I don't know where these numbers come from that say the rich get richer," the Texas Republican said.
The single biggest piece of the tax cut was a $500-per-child tax credit. The legislation also included tax breaks for college education and expanded Individual Retirement Accounts.
The House bill would cut the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from the maximum 28 percent for individuals and gradually reduce the rate for corporations to 30 percent from 35 percent.

The legislation would gradually raise the threshold where the estate tax is imposed to $1 million in 2007 from the current $600,000. The House bill would eliminate the ethanol subsidy after it expires at the end of 2000 and raise revenues from airline ticket taxes and passenger fees.

The Senate version currently amounted to a net $77 billion tax cut over five years, with a pledge from Republican leaders that it will at some point in the process be brought up to the $85 billion mark.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said he would vote for the Republican-crafted bill, despite concerns most of its benefits would flow to the wealthiest Americans. "We don't want the perfect to be the enemy of the good. There are some good things in here," the South Dakota Democrat said.
He said he hoped to work with the White House to improve the measure in coming weeks when House and Senate negotiators work out a final, compromise bill.
